summary.deep: Delegates from 69 countries meeting at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Versailles, France, have voted to abolish leap seconds. Previously used to keep Coordinated Universal Time aligned with Earth's slowing rotation, leap seconds will be abandoned because modern technological systems, including stock markets, GPS, and telecommunications, are highly sensitive to sudden time adjustments. Introducing extra seconds has historically risked crashing websites and disrupting networks. Additionally, because Earth's rotation has recently accelerated slightly, scientists faced the unprecedented prospect of implementing a negative leap second, prompting the decision to let universal time drift by up to an hour instead.
summary.std: Representatives from 69 countries voted to abolish leap seconds at a meeting of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Versailles, France. Universal time will now be allowed to drift up to an hour from astronomical time to prevent disruptions to complex modern technological systems like telecommunications and financial networks.

article.title: Scientists have just voted to abolish leap seconds

summary.brief: Pakistan faces a severe water crisis as annual groundwater extraction outpaces replenishment, leaving 80 percent of groundwater unsafe to drink.
summary.deep: Driven by an unregulated network of over 1.5 million tubewells, Pakistan is confronting a severe water and food security emergency as groundwater extraction significantly outpaces natural replenishment. According to a report by the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics, the country extracts 65 cubic kilometers of groundwater annually compared to a recharge rate of 55 cubic kilometers, making it the world's fourth-largest groundwater user. Nearly 60 percent of irrigation, over 70 percent of drinking water, and almost all industrial operations depend on this resource. Furthermore, 70 to 80 percent of the nation's groundwater is unsafe to drink, with arsenic levels threatening up to 60 million people and salinity affecting 21 percent of irrigated land. The crisis is compounded by policy biases, including subsidized electricity for tubewells and price supports for water-intensive crops like rice and sugarcane, causing water tables to drop rapidly across urban and agricultural hubs.
